title: Ch. 1 Supplemental: Who Uses the Internet?

questions.q: In the 2021 global snapshot (world population about 7.89 billion), roughly what share of the world's population were Internet users?
questions.explain: About 4.88 billion people, or 61.8% of the population, were Internet users. That is close to 5 billion people.

questions.q: In the 2021 snapshot, more people worldwide were Internet users than were unique mobile phone users.
questions.explain: Mobile phones reached more people: about 5.29 billion unique mobile phone users (67.1%), compared with about 4.88 billion Internet users (61.8%).

questions.q: About how many people, in millions, were using the Internet in the year 2000?
questions.explain: About 360 million people (0.36 billion) were online in 2000. That rose to about 1.02 billion in 2005, about 1.98 billion in 2010, and about 4.9 billion in 2021.

questions.q: From 2000 to about 2021-2022, the number of Internet users worldwide grew by roughly what factor?
questions.explain: Users grew from about 0.36 billion to nearly 5 billion, which is roughly a factor of 14-15 (the lecture rounds it to 15).

questions.q: The yearly counts of global Internet users from 1995 to 2021 show growth leveling off after about 2010.
questions.explain: Growth kept going at a fairly steady pace. Users went from about 2 billion in 2010 to about 4.6 billion in 2020 and about 4.9 billion in 2021.

questions.q: Around 1980, about how many computers were attached to the ARPANET, the Internet's predecessor?
questions.explain: Only about 200 computers were on the ARPANET in 1980. By the 2020s, nearly 5 billion people were online.

questions.q: What is the ITU, a source of global Internet-user statistics?
choices: The International Telecommunication Union, a UN specialized agency for information and communication technologies
An industry group of the largest Internet service providers
The US federal agency that funds rural broadband
The body that standardizes the TCP/IP protocols
questions.explain: The ITU is the International Telecommunication Union, a United Nations specialized agency for information and communication technologies (ICT). The worldwide counts of Internet users over time come from ITU statistics.

questions.q: In April 2021, which region had the highest Internet adoption as a percentage of its population?
questions.explain: Northern Europe was highest at 97.0%. Next came Western Europe (93.3%) and Northern America (90.4%). Eastern Asia was at 70.6%.

questions.q: In April 2021, which region had the lowest Internet adoption as a percentage of its population?
questions.explain: Eastern Africa was lowest at 24.4%. Middle Africa had 26.2%, Western Africa 40.9%, and Southern Asia 42.2%.

questions.q: In April 2021, which regions had Internet adoption above 90% of their population?
questions.explain: Northern Europe (97.0%), Western Europe (93.3%), and Northern America (90.4%) were above 90%. Southern Europe (85.7%), Eastern Europe (82.3%), and Oceania (71.0%) were below 90%.

questions.q: About how many people worldwide, in billions, were still without Internet access in 2021?
questions.explain: About 3 billion people were offline: 7.89 billion total minus about 4.88 billion users. This group is called 'the missing 3B'.

questions.q: In late 2021, which region had the largest number of people without Internet access?
questions.explain: Southern Asia had about 1,098 million people offline. Next were Eastern Asia (473 M), Eastern Africa (341 M), and Western Africa (241 M).

questions.q: Eastern Asia's adoption rate (70.6%) is far higher than Eastern Africa's (24.4%), yet Eastern Asia has more people offline (about 473 M vs. 341 M). What explains this?
choices: Eastern Asia's population is so large that even a smaller unconnected percentage adds up to more people
Adoption percentages include only mobile users, while the offline counts include only home broadband
The two statistics measure different years, so they cannot be compared at all
Eastern Africa's offline count excludes rural areas
questions.explain: A percentage and an absolute count answer different questions. In a very populous region, a 29% offline share is a huge number of people. This is why the regional rates and the 'missing 3B' counts tell different stories.

questions.q: Which definition matches 'meaningful connectivity'?
choices: Having at least one Internet-connected device in the household
The ability to use the Internet every day, on an appropriate device, with enough data and a fast connection
Living within range of at least one mobile cell tower
Having access to at least two competing ISPs
questions.explain: Meaningful connectivity asks more than whether a person is connected at all. It means daily use, an appropriate device, enough data, and a fast enough connection.

questions.q: What is the '1 for 2' Internet affordability target?
choices: 1 Mbps of bandwidth for $2 per month or less
1 GB of data for 2% or less of average monthly income
1 hour of daily Internet use for 2% of household spending
questions.explain: The target is 1 GB of data for 2% or less of average monthly income. It comes from the Alliance for Affordable Internet (A4AI).

questions.q: In 2020, about how many of 95 countries studied met the '1 for 2' affordability target?
questions.explain: 43 out of 95 countries met it, which is roughly half.

questions.q: In Colombia, basic Internet access was 84.1% with a gender gap of 0.9%, but meaningful connectivity was 50.9% with a gender gap of 16.9%. What does this illustrate?
choices: Gender gaps disappear once meaningful connectivity is measured
Simple yes/no access statistics can hide large gaps in real usability and between groups
Meaningful connectivity is always higher than basic access
Colombia's figures show that affordability is not a factor in connectivity
questions.explain: Coarse 'connected or not' numbers made Colombia look nearly fully connected and nearly gender-equal. A stricter measure of daily, adequate use shows only about half the population connected and a much larger gender gap (47.1% of women vs. 55.1% of men).

questions.q: Looking 'beyond connectivity' means examining which of the following, in addition to whether people are connected at all?
choices: The number of IP addresses allocated to each country
The number of undersea cables landing in each region
questions.explain: The deeper questions covered were meaningful connectivity, affordability (such as the '1 for 2' target), and gender gaps. Simple connected/not-connected counts are coarse-grained.

questions.q: According to the 2019 figures for Africa, roughly what share of the population was online?
questions.explain: About 29% of Africa's population was online, and mobile broadband penetration was about 30.5%. The gender gap in Internet use there was reported as 85%.

questions.q: What two-word term describes the gaps in Internet access between groups, for example by income, race, education, age, gender, or urban vs. rural location?
questions.explain: These gaps are called the digital divide. They can be measured globally (regions, gender) or within a country (US income, race, urban/rural).

questions.q: In the 2021 US data on smartphone ownership and home broadband (85% and 77% of adults overall), how did the two compare across demographic groups?
choices: Smartphone ownership varied much more across groups than home broadband
Both varied by about the same amount
Home broadband varied more across groups than smartphone ownership
questions.explain: Broadband differences were greater than smartphone differences. For example, home broadband ranged from 57% (income under $30K) to 92% (income $75K+) and from 59% (high school or less) to 94% (college+).

questions.q: In the 2021 US snapshot, which group had the lowest home broadband adoption?
questions.explain: Adults with income under $30K had the lowest rate at 57%. Adults aged 65+ were at 64%, rural adults at 72%, and adults aged 18-29 at 70%.

questions.q: In the 2021 US data, adults aged 18-29 had higher home broadband adoption than adults aged 30-49.
questions.explain: Adults aged 18-29 had the highest smartphone ownership (96%), but their home broadband rate was 70%, compared with 86% for ages 30-49.

questions.q: How has the US urban/suburban/rural gap in home broadband changed over roughly the last decade?
choices: It has widened from about 6 to more than 20 percentage points
It has narrowed from more than 20 to about 6 percentage points
It has stayed constant at about 10 percentage points
questions.explain: The rural gap has narrowed a lot but still exists. In 2021, home broadband was 79% for suburban, 77% for urban, and 72% for rural adults.

questions.q: How has the US racial digital divide in Internet adoption changed over roughly the last decade?
choices: It has narrowed as much as the rural/urban gap
It has stayed at roughly 10 percentage points without narrowing much
It has reversed, with Black and Hispanic adoption now above White adoption
questions.explain: The racial gap of about 10 points has barely narrowed. In 2018 (NTIA data), adoption was 71% for White, 62% for Hispanic, and 61% for Black Americans.

questions.q: The 2000-2018 NTIA adoption data were summarized as 'Blacks and Hispanics a decade behind.' What does that mean?
choices: Black and Hispanic adoption in 2018 (about 61-62%) was roughly where White adoption had been around 2010
Black and Hispanic Americans started using the Internet ten years after it was invented
Black and Hispanic adoption grows 10 percentage points per decade
The data for Black and Hispanic Americans are ten years out of date
questions.explain: White adoption reached about 65% around 2010. Black and Hispanic adoption did not reach a similar level (61-62%) until about 2018, so it lagged by roughly a decade.

questions.q: The 2021 US Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act allocated about $550B to infrastructure. How much of it, in billions of dollars, went to broadband?
questions.explain: $65B went to broadband, which is a bit more than a tenth of the $550B total.

questions.q: Broadband was the single largest spending category in the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act.
questions.explain: Roads and bridges were largest at $110B. Next came power infrastructure ($73B), passenger and freight rail ($66B), and then broadband ($65B).

questions.q: Which IIJA broadband program is the largest, providing about $42.5B in grants to states to expand broadband deployment in underserved areas?
questions.explain: BEAD (Broadband Equity, Access, and Deployment) is the largest piece of the $65B. The states administer the funds to build broadband where it does not yet exist.

questions.q: What does the IIJA's Affordable Connectivity Fund (about $14.2B) do?
choices: Builds new fiber backbones between states
Reimburses households up to $30/month for broadband access costs
Funds Internet access on tribal lands
Gives tax credits to ISPs for upgrading cable headends
questions.explain: It reimburses households up to $30/month for broadband access costs. Its goal is to close the income-based part of the digital divide.

questions.q: Which of these are broadband programs in the 2021 Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act?
questions.explain: The programs and amounts: BEAD ($42.5B), Affordable Connectivity Fund ($14.2B), Digital Equity ($2.75B), Tribal Broadband Connectivity ($2B), and Rural Utilities Service ReConnect ($2B). The 'National Spectrum Auction Rebate' is made up.

questions.q: What is the stated purpose of the IIJA's $2.75B Digital Equity program?
choices: To ensure individuals and communities have the IT capacity needed for full participation in US society and the economy
To pay for new mobile spectrum licenses
To fund broadband only on tribal lands
To reimburse ISPs for unpaid customer bills
questions.explain: Digital Equity funds the IT capacity people need to take full part in US society and the economy. Tribal lands are covered by the separate $2B Tribal Broadband Connectivity Program.

questions.q: In January 2021, what was the most commonly cited primary reason that global Internet users aged 16-64 use the Internet?
choices: Watching videos, TV shows, and movies
Staying in touch with friends and family
questions.explain: Finding information was first at 63.0%. Next came staying in touch with friends and family (56.3%) and keeping up with news and events (55.6%).

questions.q: Which of these primary reasons for using the Internet were cited by more than half of global users aged 16-64 (January 2021)?
choices: Staying in touch with friends and family
Keeping up to date with news and events
Watching videos, TV shows, and movies
questions.explain: Above 50%: finding information (63.0%), staying in touch (56.3%), news and events (55.6%), researching how to do things (51.9%), and watching videos/TV/movies (51.7%). Below 50%: music (46.3%) and gaming (32.2%).

questions.q: Meeting new people was among the most popular reasons for using the Internet, cited by more users than finding information.
questions.explain: Meeting new people was at the bottom of the list shown, at 29.9%. Finding information was at the top with 63.0%.

questions.q: In January 2021, which country had the highest average mobile Internet download speed?
questions.explain: The UAE was highest at about 177.5 Mbps. South Korea (about 169 Mbps) and China (about 156 Mbps) came next.

questions.q: In January 2021, what was the average US mobile download speed, in Mbps?
questions.explain: The US average was about 67.3 Mbps. That is far from the top (UAE at 177.5 Mbps) but above the worldwide average of about 42.7 Mbps.

questions.q: In January 2021, the average US mobile download speed was above the worldwide average.
questions.explain: The US average was about 67.3 Mbps, compared with about 42.7 Mbps worldwide. Several countries were slower still, for example India at about 12.9 Mbps.

questions.q: In a speed test from a home on Comcast cable in western Massachusetts to a Comcast server in Boston, what path do the packets take?
choices: Home network -> cable access network -> cable headend -> Comcast router/network -> server
Home network -> DSL line -> telephone central office -> alter.net -> server
Home network -> Verizon wireless network -> alter.net -> Comcast network -> server
Home network -> cable headend -> a different ISP's backbone -> server
questions.explain: Packets go from the home network over the shared cable access network to the cable headend. A Comcast router there forwards them through Comcast's network to the server. The whole path is Comcast, and no other ISP is involved.

questions.q: In the home cable speed test to the Boston Comcast server, the packets had to cross at least one other ISP's network.
questions.explain: The home connects directly to Comcast's Xfinity cable network, and the server is a Comcast server. The test packets never leave Comcast's network.

questions.q: The home cable connection measured about 300 Mbps download but only about 17 Mbps upload. Why is cable access engineered to be so asymmetric?
choices: Upload traffic must be encrypted, which slows it down
Residential users mostly consume data (for example, streaming video) rather than produce it, so more capacity goes to the downstream direction
The speed test server in Boston could not receive data faster than 17 Mbps
Upstream signals travel a longer physical distance than downstream signals
questions.explain: Home users are mainly consumers of data: they download much more than they upload. The ISP builds the cable access network to match, giving downstream far more capacity than upstream.

questions.q: The cable speed test measured about 300 Mbps download and about 17 Mbps upload. Roughly what is the ratio of download to upload speed?
questions.explain: 300 / 17 is about 17.6. The lecture rounds this to roughly a factor of 20.

questions.q: For the speed test from an iPhone on Verizon's wireless network to the Boston Comcast server, which networks did the packets traverse?
choices: Verizon wireless network -> Comcast network, directly
Verizon wireless network -> alter.net -> Comcast network
Verizon wireless network -> cable headend -> alter.net -> Comcast network
questions.explain: The packets had to be forwarded between Verizon's network and Comcast's network. One intermediate network, alter.net, sat on the path between them.

questions.q: How did the mobile (Verizon) download speed to the Boston server compare with the wired home cable download speed?
choices: Mobile was about 2 Mbps vs. over 300 Mbps on cable
Mobile was about 177 Mbps vs. about 300 Mbps on cable
Mobile and cable were both about 300 Mbps
Mobile was faster, about 500 Mbps vs. 300 Mbps on cable
questions.explain: The mobile test reached only about 2 Mbps, compared with over 300 Mbps on the wired cable connection. Access speed depends heavily on the access network used.
